title: The Prydwen
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 11 of 40
content:
The Prydwen smelled like hot metal, hydraulic fluid, and too many people living above the ground.

That last part was what unsettled me.

In the Commonwealth, buildings stayed where they had been built. Even ruined ones had the decency to be attached to the earth. The Prydwen hummed beneath my boots. Engines vibrated through every bulkhead. Somewhere beyond the walls, Boston moved far below us.

Danse, naturally, looked comfortable.

He led me through the main deck with the particular pride of someone showing me a home he had spent weeks pretending not to miss.

“Flight deck is aft. Medical is one level down. Proctor Teagan handles supplies. Proctor Ingram oversees power armor maintenance and engineering.”

“Do I get a map?”

“You’ll learn.”

“That means no.”

“It means pay attention.”

Every few steps someone saluted him.

Danse returned each one without slowing.

I watched people’s faces when they recognized him. Respect, mostly. Relief. A few smiles. One knight clapped him on the shoulder and said he had heard Gladius was in bad shape.

Danse’s expression did not change.

“We completed the mission.”

The knight’s smile faded.

Only after we passed did I realize what Danse had done. He had turned four deaths into a sentence he could carry.

I wanted to touch his arm.

I did not.

We reached the command deck.

Elder Arthur Maxson was younger than I expected and somehow looked older because of it. A long coat hung from his shoulders. A scar cut across one side of his face. He carried authority differently than Danse. Danse wore command like a responsibility. Maxson wore it like a natural law.

His speech was exactly as dramatic as I had been promised.

Humanity. Technology. Duty. The Institute beneath the Commonwealth like a disease.

I listened.

I also watched Danse.

His attention never wandered.

This was faith, I realized.

Not religious exactly. But the same architecture: a story explaining suffering, a community giving it meaning, a set of rules promising that if people were disciplined enough the world might stop ending.

When Maxson addressed me, I answered carefully.

Danse had vouched for me.

That mattered more than the uniform they eventually handed me.

Afterward he took me to the observation deck.

Boston stretched below the rail in the blue-gray distance. The city looked almost peaceful from this height. I could not see bodies. Could not smell rot. Could not hear settlers arguing over water.

“Impressive,” I admitted.

Danse rested his forearms on the rail.

“I told you.”

“You did.”

“Do I get to hear you say I was right?”

I looked at him.

“Are you developing a sense of humor?”

“I’ve always had one.”

“Evidence is limited.”

He shook his head.

For a few minutes we stood in companionable silence.

Then I asked, “Are you happy?”

The question surprised him.

“I’m relieved.”

“That wasn’t what I asked.”

“You do that a lot.”

“What?”

“Refuse the practical answer.”

“Someone has to.”

Danse looked out at the horizon.

“Yes,” he said eventually. “I’m happy.”

The admission softened his whole face.

“I thought we might never make it back. Every week in Cambridge, supplies got lower. The antenna got worse. My people…”

He stopped.

“I know.”

“I kept telling them command would answer.”

“And they did.”

“Yes.”

He breathed out.

“For once.”

That last phrase was so quiet I almost missed it.

I looked at him.

Danse stared over the rail as if he had said nothing.

Before I could ask, an alarm sounded from the deck below. Not an emergency—shift change.

He straightened immediately.

“I need to report to Kells.”

“Go.”

“You know how to find the quarters?”

“No.”

He sighed.

“I’ll take you.”

“I can ask someone.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

His expression suggested the answer should be obvious.

“Because you’re my responsibility.”

I folded my arms.

“I thought I was a recruit.”

“You can be both.”

“Dangerous sentence.”

He realized it a second too late.

The tips of his ears turned faintly red.

I treasured the discovery.

The sleeping quarters were narrow rows of bunks beneath pipes and tanks I preferred not to identify.

Danse indicated an empty bed.

“This is yours.”

I looked up at the machinery overhead.

“What’s in those?”

“Hydrogen.”

I stared at him.

He maintained a perfectly serious expression for almost three seconds.

Then the corner of his mouth betrayed him.

“You’re joking.”

“Mostly.”

“Mostly?”

“You’ll get used to sleeping under highly flammable infrastructure.”

“That is not comforting.”

“It wasn’t intended to be.”

There it was again: the hidden humor, dry enough to miss if I expected him to announce it.

I sat on the bunk.

Danse lingered.

“Something else?” I asked.

“No.”

He did not move.

“Paladin.”

“I wanted to make certain you were settled.”

“I have a mattress and a ceiling full of explosive gas. I’m living extravagantly.”

His smile came easier this time.

“Get some rest.”

“You too.”

“I have a debriefing.”

“After.”

He gave me the command look.

I gave it back.

It was less effective coming from a bunk.

“I’ll try,” he said.

That was enough.

He turned to leave.

“Danse.”

He stopped.

“Thanks for bringing me here.”

For a second the Prydwen, the Brotherhood, the ranks and orders all seemed to fall away.

His expression became unexpectedly gentle.

“I’m glad you came.”

Then he left.

I lay back beneath the pipes and listened to the airship breathe.

For the first time in years, I was sleeping somewhere that moved.

For the first time in almost as long, I found the thought less frightening because I knew exactly who was somewhere nearby.

The first thing the Prydwen taught me was that Danse had a reputation.

Not the kind people whispered about.

The kind they straightened for.

We had barely cleared medical screening when a young initiate carrying a stack of parts spotted him in the corridor.

“Paladin Danse, sir.”

Danse stopped.

The initiate snapped to attention so quickly one of the parts slid off the stack. I caught it before it hit the deck.

“Easy,” I said.

The initiate looked horrified that I had spoken during whatever ritual this was.

Danse took the component from me and placed it back on the pile.

“At ease. What’s your assignment?”

“Flight deck maintenance, sir.”

“Then get those to Proctor Ingram before she sends someone looking for you.”

“Yes, sir.”

The initiate hurried away.

I waited until we were alone.

“You terrify children.”

“He is nineteen.”

“Ancient.”

“He’s an initiate.”

“That wasn’t my point.”

Danse resumed walking.

“He served with a Capital Wasteland patrol during training. Competent. Too eager to impress.”

“You know him?”

“I know my people.”

That answer changed the ship around me.

Until then the Brotherhood had been uniforms and ranks and steel. Danse saw individual soldiers inside it. He knew who rushed, who froze, who needed another week on maintenance, who could be trusted with a difficult watch.

We passed the mess, the armory, sleeping quarters stacked with military efficiency. He greeted people by name. They greeted him by rank.

Some asked about Cambridge.

Every time, something in his shoulders tightened.

“Recon Squad Gladius suffered heavy losses,” he said to one knight.

Not *Brach cheated at cards.*

Not *Worwick sang badly.*

Heavy losses.

The language of reports turned people back into numbers because numbers could be carried in public without bleeding through the uniform.

At the observation window near the bow, Danse stopped.

The Commonwealth lay beneath cloud and evening haze.

“You can return to the surface if this is uncomfortable,” he said.

I leaned on the railing.

“You’ve said that three times.”

“The Prydwen is a military vessel.”

“I noticed the giant guns.”

“I mean you are not obligated to remain here.”

There it was again.

The careful exit he kept building for me.

“Do you want me to leave?”

His answer took too long.

“No.”

“Then stop trying to dismiss me politely.”

“I’m not dismissing you.”

“You’re pre-rejecting yourself on my behalf.”

His brow furrowed.

“That phrase makes no sense.”

“It makes perfect sense.”

“It does not.”

“Danse.”

His eyes shifted at the use of his name without rank.

I lowered my voice.

A group of initiates passed us, laughing too loudly until they noticed Danse and straightened in near-perfect unison.

He returned their salutes. They hurried on.

“That happens often?” I asked.

“What?”

“People becoming six inches taller when you walk by.”

“Discipline.”

“Fear.”

“Respect.”

“Terrified respect.”

He almost smiled.

Then his expression turned thoughtful as he watched the initiates disappear around the bend.

“I was like that once.”

“You?”

“Yes.”

“Impossible. I assumed you emerged fully formed from a suit of T-60 armor.”

“That would explain several things.”

I laughed. He did too, barely.

It was easy to forget the Brotherhood had once been new to him. Once he had been a scrap trader from Rivet City trying to learn where to stand, how to salute, how to become useful enough to stay. The Prydwen did not merely represent authority.

It represented the first place that had given his life a shape.

“I know this place matters to you. I know I don’t belong here the way you do. I’m still choosing to be here.”

The engines vibrated through the deck under our boots.

He looked out the window.

“Choice can change when circumstances do.”

“Yes.”

“And if it does?”

“I’ll tell you.”

He nodded once.

A soldier’s acceptance of terms.

Then, softer, “All right.”

We stood beside each other watching Boston pass beneath us.

A minute later an officer rounded the corner and Danse’s spine snapped straight again.

The private moment vanished.

But not before I had learned something important.

He did not assume people stayed.

He merely hoped they would and tried very hard not to make the hope visible.
